title: Final Review
description: Blind tasting, label reading and pairing: everything the previous twenty-nine modules taught.
L: Explain how to approach a blind tasting
Use evidence from appearance, nose and palate

Blind tasting is reasoning, not guessing. Gather evidence: colour, aroma intensity and families, structure. Then ask what it suggests. Deep colour suggests thick skins or warmth. High acidity suggests a cool climate or a high-acid grape. Oak suggests ambition and price. Each clue narrows the options.

Build the argument in steps. Is it Old World or New World? Fruit-forward and ripe suggests New World or warm sites; earthy, savoury and restrained suggests Old World or cool sites. Then climate: cool, moderate or warm. Then grape. Then region and age. Stop when the evidence runs out, rather than forcing an answer.
A red is pale ruby, high acidity, low tannin, red cherry and earthy notes. What is the most likely conclusion?
Pale colour, low tannin, high acidity and earthiness point to a cool-climate Pinot Noir, like Burgundy.
In blind tasting, the first impression is often right, but say why. If you can't justify a guess with evidence from the glass, keep looking.
Put the steps of a blind conclusion in order.
Decide Old World or New World
Each step narrows the possibilities using the evidence before it.

Use structure as much as aroma

Sauvignon Blanc: pronounced grass, gooseberry, high acidity, no oak. Riesling: lime, flowers, high acidity, sometimes sugar and petrol. Chardonnay: neutral fruit shaped by place and oak, often butter and toast. Gewürztraminer: lychee, rose, low acidity, high alcohol. Chenin Blanc: apple, quince, honey, high acidity.

Cabernet Sauvignon: blackcurrant, cedar, high tannin. Merlot: plum, softer tannin. Pinot Noir: pale, red fruit, low tannin. Syrah: blackberry, pepper, deep colour. Nebbiolo: pale but very tannic, rose and tar. Sangiovese: sour cherry, high acidity, tea-like tannin. Structure often reveals more than aroma.
Tannin and acidity reveal the grape
Match each wine description to its grape.
Sour cherry, high acidity, tea tannin
Combining aroma and structure gives the clearest identification.

Some grapes are easily confused. Pinot Noir and Gamay are both pale and red-fruited; Gamay is often juicier, with banana notes from carbonic maceration. Cabernet and Merlot blend so often it's hard to separate them. Albariño and Grüner Veltliner both show citrus and acidity; Grüner adds white pepper.
A wine that is pale in colour must be low in tannin.
Not true. Nebbiolo is pale but very tannic, a classic blind tasting trap.
Each white grape has an aroma plus acidity fingerprint
Red grapes are often identified by tannin and acidity
Know the common confusions, like Pinot Noir and Gamay
Use climate clues to identify regions

Regions leave marks through climate. Chablis Chardonnay is lean and steely; Californian Chardonnay is riper with more oak. Mosel Riesling is light and off-dry; Clare Valley Riesling is dry with lime. Bordeaux Cabernet is cedar and restraint; Napa is ripe and powerful.

Winemaking traditions also point to regions. American oak's coconut and vanilla suggest traditional Rioja. Long lees ageing and toast suggest Champagne. Carbonic maceration's banana suggests Beaujolais. Dried grape character with high alcohol suggests Amarone. Flor's tangy, nutty character means Fino or Manzanilla.
Match each clue to its likely region.
Regional traditions shape flavour as much as grape.

A lean, mineral, unoaked Chardonnay at 12.5% points to Chablis. A powerful, ripe Cabernet at 14.5% with sweet oak points to Napa. A Sauvignon Blanc with pronounced passion fruit points to Marlborough; with restraint and flint, to Sancerre. Use every clue: climate, grape, winemaking and structure.
A Sauvignon Blanc with intense passion fruit and grass, very high acidity and no oak. Which region is most likely?
Pronounced passion fruit and grass with high acidity is classic Marlborough. Sancerre is more restrained; Pessac-Léognan is often oaked.
Climate leaves its mark on the same grape
Combine climate, grape, winemaking and structure
Choose wines for a full menu

When in doubt: match weight; wine as sweet as the food; acidic food needs acidic wine; salt and fat love acidity and bubbles; tannin needs fat or protein; chilli needs low alcohol and a touch of sugar; umami needs fruity, low-tannin wines. These rules cover most dishes.

Artichokes and asparagus contain compounds that make wine taste sweet or metallic; choose crisp, unoaked whites like Grüner Veltliner or Sauvignon Blanc. Eggs coat the palate; try Champagne. Chocolate needs sweet, fortified wine, like Banyuls or tawny Port. Very spicy curries suit off-dry Riesling.
Match each dish to a strong choice.
These pairings follow the core principles.
For a menu with many dishes, a versatile wine like dry Champagne, Pinot Noir or a dry Riesling will rarely clash. Bubbles and acidity forgive a lot.
Which wines are generally versatile across many dishes?
Very tannic reds clash with many foods, especially fish, umami and chilli.
Remember the core rules: weight, sweetness, acidity, tannin, heat
Versatile wines like Champagne and Pinot Noir suit mixed menus

A botrytised sweet wine like Sauternes

Match each wine to its key process.
Every great wine style comes from a process you've learned.
Which label terms show minimum ageing?
Brut is about sweetness; an aged tawny's indication is an average style, not a strict minimum age.
A pale red with high tannin and rose and tar aromas is most likely Nebbiolo.
Yes. Pale colour with high tannin is Nebbiolo's signature.
